tagline.text: Forests and grassy ridges at Mindoro's northwestern tip, home to the tamaraw

location.label: Location
location.text: Barangays Harrison, Alipaoy and Mananao, Paluan, Occidental Mindoro

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱2,000~5,000 (excluding round-trip transport from Manila; estimate for local transport, guide and meals)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Walk-in by land from Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL) in Manila or San Jose Airport (SJI)

children.text: Mount Calavite Wildlife Sanctuary is a protected area of about 18,000 hectares in Paluan, at the northwestern tip of Mindoro Island. Forests and grasslands shelter the critically endangered tamaraw and Mindoro's endemic birds, and from near the summit you can look out over the sea and the Lubang Islands.

Mount Calavite rises on Cape Calavite, the headland at the northwestern tip of Mindoro Island. It lies north of the town proper of Paluan in Occidental Mindoro, and its height varies slightly by source, from about 1,491 m to 1,521 m; the most widely used figure is 1,521 m. About 18,000 hectares around the mountain (18,016 or 18,172 hectares, depending on the source) are designated as the Mount Calavite Wildlife Sanctuary, spanning the three barangays of Harrison, Alipaoy and Mananao.

The area was first declared a game refuge and bird sanctuary in 1920 to protect the habitat of the tamaraw (Mindoro dwarf buffalo), which lives only on Mindoro. In 1925 the mountain and the neighboring area of Harrison village were proclaimed a national park, and in 2000 Presidential Proclamation No. 292 made it the wildlife sanctuary it is today. Only three places on Mindoro are known to still hold tamaraws, and Mount Calavite is one of them.

What kind of destination this is should be clear from the start. It is not a beach resort or a place with well-developed tourist facilities; it is a hiking destination of forest trails and grassy ridges inside a protected area. The Occidental Mindoro provincial tourism site likewise describes it as not a typical trekking and camping destination, and stresses conservation of the sanctuary. The upside is that it is quiet and uncrowded, and as you climb, the town of Paluan and the sea stay spread out behind you.

One thing to know first: do not expect to see a tamaraw. A June 2019 survey led by the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) found tracks, dung and signs of grazing, and estimated that there might be 4 to 6 animals. According to a 2023 local report, a separate camera-trap study had not yet found confirmed evidence. Think of this trip not as an animal-spotting trip but as a chance to walk through a rare habitat on foot.

blocks.title: A summit view from Mindoro's northwestern headland

children.text: Near the top the view opens in every direction. To the northeast you see the Batangas and Calatagan side, to the east the mountain ranges of Oriental Mindoro, and to the west the South China Sea and the Lubang Islands. Climbers' records say Mount Halcon was visible on clear days.

The tamaraw is a critically endangered buffalo found only on Mindoro. This is one of the three remaining habitats on the island, and the sanctuary has also been mentioned as a candidate site for a breeding program that would relocate animals from Mounts Iglit-Baco National Park. The chance of meeting one is low, but the habitat itself is what makes this mountain valuable.

The sanctuary is described as home to the Mindoro bleeding-heart, Mindoro hornbill, Mindoro hawk-owl, spotted imperial pigeon, scarlet-collared flowerpecker and more. Forest trails at dawn are best for watching, and binoculars help.

The start is a grove of chestnut trees, followed soon by a steep forest trail. From about 700 m above sea level the scenery changes to shrubland with wild strawberries and open grassy ridges. There are records of horses and carabao grazing in the grass.

An Iraya Mangyan community lives in Sitio Ulasan, the trailhead village. Guides and porters are said to be available there, so the hike also brings income to the village. Greet people and respect local ways.

blocks.title: Agbokbok Falls and the waters of Paluan

children.text: Agbokbok Falls inside the sanctuary is known to nature lovers, and Paluan has several other waterfalls, including Bisay Falls. Many visitors add a stream rinse-off after the hike. Check on site how to reach the falls and what condition they are in.

blocks.title: A quiet trip in western Mindoro

children.text: Unlike Puerto Galera, this side of the island sees very few tourists. It pairs well with a look at Paluan town and the Mananao coast for quiet countryside scenery.

The day hike is recommended only for strong hikers. A same-day round trip from Manila is not realistic; the safer plan is to sleep a night in Paluan and start early in the morning.

items.subtitle: Sleep at base camp and greet the summit sunrise

children.text: Start the hike from Sitio Ulasan. Have lunch near Sam's viewdeck.
Arrive at the base camp, where water is available, and pitch your tent. The state of the water varies by season, so ask your local guide.
Leave your gear and climb lightly toward the summit, returning before evening. A record says it takes about
1 hour 30 minutes
to reach the old transmitter tower just below the top.
Wake up, have breakfast and pack.
Start down and reach the village after about
2 hours 30 minutes

Take a van to Abra de Ilog and catch an afternoon ferry. Be sure to check the ferry schedule.
Check first with the protected area office (PAMB) and the town hall whether camping is allowed. Camping without permission is not recommended.

One account says the trip from Manila to Paluan takes about
10 hours

items.title: From Manila by air and road

children.text: Flights are said to operate from Manila to San Jose (SJI) Airport. From the airport, however, you still face another long ride by land to Paluan.
From the Mamburao integrated terminal you can take a van or jeepney to Paluan.
Register at Paluan town hall, then hire a tricycle through Harrison village to the entrance of Sitio Ulasan. It takes about
30 minutes
A 2008 record gave ₱150 per trip (up to 5 people). Getting the driver's number is handy for arranging a pickup after the hike.

Hiking is better in the dry season, when the trail is firm. The dry season is generally December to May, but it varies from year to year, so check the weather before you leave. The grassy sections have no shade and get hot by day, and wind and cloud can sweep in suddenly near the summit.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: Known as the best time for hiking. Mornings and evenings can be chilly.
Direct sun is strong on the grassy sections. Start early and bring plenty of water.
Rainy season, heaviest in July and August
Trails are slippery and streams swell. Hiking is not recommended; check the weather.

items.label: Accommodation
items.note: Mostly small lodgings in Paluan town

items.label: Meals

Paluan is a small coastal town with few lodgings and restaurants. There are small guesthouses and resorts, and Mamburao has more varied accommodation. Most people sleep in Paluan the night before the hike, so contact places ahead of time. Rooms can run short in peak season or during events.

Restaurants are mostly simple eateries around the town market. There are no restaurants on the mountain, so buy a packed lunch, snacks and plenty of water in the village. A 2008 climbing record said water is available near the base camp, but purify any drinking water.
Before your visit, ask the Paluan town hall or the sanctuary office about hike permission, registration and arranging a guide. The contact number in the 2008 record is old and may no longer connect.
Guides are said to be available from the Iraya Mangyan community in Sitio Ulasan. Part of the trail is covered by grass, so go with a guide.
Leave plenty of buffer in ferry and van connections, and if touts at Abra de Ilog offer a van via Mamburao, check whether a direct van is available.
The grassy sections have no shade. Bring a hat, sunscreen and 2 to 3 liters of water.
A record says Globe signal reaches the entire trail, but that may differ now. Download maps in advance.
Do not chase wildlife, and carry out all your trash. This is a protected area, so collecting and hunting are prohibited.
Wear hiking boots with good grip rather than city shoes, and check the forecast and sunset time so you start down early in the afternoon.
Current trail conditions and permit procedures are hardly documented in public sources. Be sure to check beforehand with the Paluan town hall or the sanctuary office, and avoid hiking alone.
Many of the fares and times in this guide come from a 2008 climbing record and may differ from today's reality.
Near the summit the trail can vanish under grass. Follow the ridge, and turn back if visibility is poor.
In the rainy season the trail is slippery and heavy rain can make stream crossings difficult.
There are no restaurants or safety facilities on the mountain. Bring first-aid supplies and spare drinking water.
This is tamaraw habitat. If you meet an animal, do not approach it and keep your distance.

blocks.title: Paluan town and the Mananao coast

children.text: Paluan village below the mountain sits on the northeastern shore of Paluan Bay. It is a good place for a market visit and a shoreline stroll before or after the hike.
Paluan is known for its many waterfalls. For falls inside the sanctuary, check on site how to get there.
These are the islands you can see across the sea to the west from the summit. A separate boat is needed, so confirm the schedule locally.
Western Mindoro's leading dive site, reached by boat from the Sablayan side. It is far from Paluan, so plan it as a separate trip.
